title: P23A — one verified backup, one total loss of the database, one restore, and the audited truth that came back and kept going
problem: P22 closed with a real POST /customers committing over live HTTP inside the frozen deploy artifact — and with the database that carried it deleted at the end of the run. Nothing had ever been taken OUT of that database and put back. So the one question every business asks about its own data had no answer in this repository at all: if the database is lost, does the truth come back, and does it come back complete — the migration head, the exact rows, the non-superuser roles, the forced row-level security and a hash-chained audit trail that still verifies? An untested backup is not a backup, and a restore nobody has ever performed is a hope, not a capability. Worse, the failure path had never been seen either: nobody knew whether the still-running listener, holding a credential to a database that no longer exists, fails closed or leaks what it holds.
solution: One recovery seam, tests/_harness/live-recovery-probe.mjs, is added BESIDE the two P22 harnesses and changes no byte of either. It starts no environment, defines no image, publishes no port and puts no credential on a command line: it is handed the ONE environment P22B1 already builds, and every HTTP request, verification read and trusted principal comes from the UNCHANGED P22B2 probe. captureBackup takes a custom-format archive of exactly the mfk database, inside the database's own container as the local superuser over its trusted socket, and writes it for its owner alone with a recomputable sha256. databaseReachable asks the same bounded question before and after the disaster. destroyDatabase removes the database container AND the data volume under it, then verifies both absences against the daemon. restoreDatabase re-hashes the archive before creating anything, brings up a FRESH volume served by the SAME pinned image under the same run label so the unchanged P22B1 teardown still removes it, re-creates the two non-superuser roles a one-database archive cannot carry — with the runtime password read from the credential file the listener is still holding, crossing on psql's stdin — and loads the archive with --exit-on-error so a partial restore can never be reported as a recovery. The fresh cluster's own superuser password is never an environment variable of the restored container: it is written RAW into a mode-0600 file, bind-mounted read-only at /run/secrets/postgres-password, and named to the image by path through POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE, so the only POSTGRES_PASSWORD* entry docker inspect can ever return is a path. The host file is deleted only after the restored cluster really answers, because the image reads it during initdb. The frozen test then judges the recovery by the server: the rows read back before the loss are compared to the rows read back after it, and the post-restore write must chain onto the entry hash the genesis had BEFORE the disaster.

acceptanceScenarios.title: the recovery seam and its package contract exist, fix a credential-free custom dump and a pinned restore, bind the package, and preserve all six P22 surfaces byte-identical
acceptanceScenarios.asserts: The probe exports exactly RECOVERY_PROBE_CONTRACT, captureBackup, databaseReachable, destroyDatabase and restoreDatabase; the contract is frozen and fixes the mfk database, the postgres backup role, the custom format, mode 0600, no credential on a command line, no published host port, the db alias and the two non-superuser roles; all four timeout bounds are finite, positive and no looser than the P22B1 environment's own; the contract names exactly the six preserved surfaces with exactly their recorded digests and each still hashes to that digest in the working tree; the probe source defines no image, runs nothing privileged, publishes no port, holds no password in an environment variable, never dumps the whole cluster and carries no importable reference to the environment harness; and this manifest records the base, the pinned Actionplan budget, the recomputed frozen-test digest, the three scope hashes with the synthesis text they were taken from, the three allowed files, the measured metrics inside the class ceiling with the conditional band and all seven gates, the rollback with every untouched surface, the twenty-seven-flag readiness set, the declared non-goals, the capability delta, both product claims and the five Turkish owner-facing fields.

acceptanceScenarios.title: one trusted write commits over live HTTP, and the environment yields a credential-free custom-format backup of exactly that database whose digest, owner-only mode and capture instant are all independently recomputable
acceptanceScenarios.asserts: All four runtime tables start empty exactly as P22B1 leaves them; one trusted POST /customers answers 201 with a COMMITTED receipt bound to that exact request; each business table then holds exactly the one row the receipt names under the trusted tenant, and the single decision row verifies independently as the genesis of that tenant's chain carrying this request's own trace id; and the backup descriptor is frozen, records the mfk database taken by the postgres role in custom format at mode 0600, lands in the directory it was given, matches the file's real size, really is mode 0600 on disk, carries the sha256 of the bytes really written, begins with the PGDMP magic of a real PostgreSQL custom archive, contains the live runtime credential nowhere, and records a capture instant that really falls between the call and its return.

acceptanceScenarios.title: destroying the database container AND its data volume is a total loss that the still-running listener fails closed on, without leaking the credential it still holds
acceptanceScenarios.asserts: The database is reachable before the loss; the frozen loss descriptor names and really removes both the container and the volume; the database is then unreachable, the container is gone from the daemon rather than stopped, no superuser verification read still succeeds and the labelled volume no longer exists; the application container is still running and its mounted credential is still the live one; and a write sent into that loss fails closed with a 5xx carrying no CommitReceipt, claiming no commit, and disclosing neither the runtime password nor any connection string.

acceptanceScenarios.title: restoring the backup into a fresh volume served by the SAME pinned image brings back the migration head, the exact four-table truth, the non-superuser roles with row-level security still forced, and a chain that still verifies
acceptanceScenarios.asserts: The frozen restore descriptor names the same pinned image and container as the lost database, the mfk database and a volume that is NOT the destroyed one, with a canonical restore instant; the running container is the pinned image, publishes no host port, is attached to exactly the one internal network, its Config.Env carries exactly one POSTGRES_PASSWORD* entry and that entry is POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/postgres-password, and its whole inspect output carries no POSTGRES_PASSWORD= at all, neither the runtime credential nor any connection string; the restored database stands at exactly migration head 0003_policy_decision_log; every business table holds exactly the rows it held before the loss and the decision log holds exactly the one genesis, same id, same entry hash, still head of the chain and still verifying independently by recomputation from the payload that came back out of the archive; both roles come back non-superuser, NOBYPASSRLS, NOCREATEDB and NOCREATEROLE with login; every runtime table comes back with row-level security enabled AND forced and its tenant-isolation policy in place; and the restored runtime role is still refused DDL by PostgreSQL itself with SQLSTATE 42501.

acceptanceScenarios.title: a second trusted write after the restore commits and chains onto the restored genesis, and the UNCHANGED P22B1 teardown leaves zero labelled resources and no backup on disk
acceptanceScenarios.asserts: The listener, never restarted and never re-credentialed, reaches the restored database through the same mounted file on the same alias and commits a second customer; each business table then holds the restored row AND the new one in that order; the log holds exactly two rows and the second chains onto the entry hash the genesis had BEFORE the disaster, recording an allowed decision; and after the unchanged P22B1 teardown no labelled container, network, image tag, volume or secret directory survives — including the container and the fresh volume the RESTORE created — and the backup directory is gone from disk.

splitEvidence.scopeSynthesisText: P23A is one backup, one total loss and one restore, proven end to end inside the SAME unchanged P22B1 environment. In scope: one credential-free custom-format dump of exactly the mfk database with a recomputable sha256, an owner-only file mode and a real capture instant; the destruction of the database container AND its data volume, so the loss is total, with the still-running listener required to fail closed without leaking the credential it still holds; the restore of that archive into a FRESH volume served by the SAME pinned image, bringing back the migration head, the exact four-table truth, the two non-superuser roles, forced row-level security with tenant-isolation policies, and an independently verifiable decision chain; and one further trusted write that commits and chains onto the restored genesis before the UNCHANGED P22B1 teardown leaves zero labelled resources behind. Out of scope, explicitly and permanently for this package: high availability, failover, migration or upgrade rollback, point-in-time recovery, WAL archiving, any agreed RPO or RTO, any scheduled or offsite backup, any production or staging environment, any registry or deployment, any host port, any image definition, any roadmap edit and any dependency or CI change. Exactly three files change: the frozen test, one new recovery probe beside the two P22 harnesses, and this manifest.
splitEvidence.parentScopeText: P23 is the HA/DR/upgrade-rollback production-proof phase: no high-availability, disaster-recovery or upgrade-rollback drill exists yet. P23A is the first package inside it and takes only the disaster-recovery backup-and-restore proof; the remaining P23 work stays outstanding and is not claimed here.
splitEvidence.blindScopeText: One recovery seam beside the two P22 harnesses: take a verified backup of the one business database, destroy that database totally, restore it into a fresh volume served by the same pinned image, and prove by reading the server that the audited truth came back complete and that the business continued on the same hash chain — starting no environment, defining no image and putting no credential on a command line.
splitEvidence.blindScopeDetermination: The blind scope was frozen and hashed from the same immutable base aa15580462d6d261e693c0c617fcac15f75be593 before either side saw the other; P23A_SCOPE_SYNTHESIS_V1 is the reconciled result and is the only scope this package was written against.

remainingOwnership.P23B: upgrade and migration rollback drill: a schema version moved forward and then really taken back, which P23A explicitly does not attempt
remainingOwnership.P23C: high-availability and failover proof: more than one instance, a lost node and traffic that survives it — no part of which exists yet
remainingOwnership.P23D: roadmap current-truth closure for P23, and the phase counter that moves only when the whole phase closes

splitEvidence.counterUnmovedReason: P23A is one package inside the already-active P23 phase. A proven restore is a capability, not a phase completion: P23 is HA, DR and upgrade rollback together, and two thirds of that is still outstanding. The counter moves when P23D closes P23 in the roadmap current truth, and this package edits no roadmap document.

budget.measurement: git diff --numstat against base tree 136dfe6c766630efbceffd5842b209c1ff0b24d8, counting the three allowed files and nothing else; no existing file is modified, so gross deletions are zero and net equals gross additions.

conditionalDeliveryGates.evidence: One problem only: is there a verified backup of this system's business database, does a total loss of that database behave safely, and does a restore really bring the audited truth back complete and continuable? No high availability, no failover, no migration or upgrade rollback, no point-in-time recovery, no WAL archiving, no recovery objective, no schedule, no offsite copy, no second environment and no roadmap edit.

Exactly three files, declared in allowedFiles before the first write and unchanged since. One is the frozen test the writer did not author and did not edit; the other two are new, and one of them is test-only harness code. No src module, no host module, no image file, no schema, no migration, no dependency and no workflow is touched, and the six preserved surfaces are proven byte-identical by the frozen test itself.

Nothing is reimplemented. The environment is P22B1's, unchanged and read-only; every HTTP request, verification read and trusted principal is P22B2's, unchanged; the independent verification of each persisted decision row is the production verifyPersistedDecisionLogRow; the archive is produced and loaded by PostgreSQL's own pg_dump and pg_restore rather than by any serialization this package wrote; and the teardown that must remove the restored container and its fresh volume is the P22B1 teardown, reached by giving them the run's own label instead of adding a second sweep.

The probe fails closed everywhere it could be tempted to claim success: an empty dump, an archive whose sha256 no longer matches, a restore reporting any error under --exit-on-error, or a database that never becomes reachable inside its bound is an exception naming what was attempted, never a descriptor. The recovery introduces no credential exposure of its own: no password is a command-line argument, none is an environment variable of any container it starts, and the restored cluster's superuser password reaches the image only as a mode-0600 read-only mounted file named by path. Every descriptor it returns is frozen. No credential is ever a command-line argument: the dump runs over the container's own trusted socket, the restored role passwords cross on psql's stdin, and the new cluster's own password reaches the daemon in a mode-0600 file deleted as soon as the container exists. The loss is verified against the daemon rather than inferred from an exit status, and the restore is judged by rows read back from the server rather than by anything the probe reports about itself.

Targeted RED-to-GREEN plus the two narrow P22 regressions are the writer's; one full local QA run is the writer's single budgeted execution and the CI full run is the second. Each re-spend is a REPLACEMENT and never an additional run: the restore's secret boundary changed once — the superuser password moved off --env-file and onto a read-only mounted mode-0600 file — and the port oracle changed once more, and each change invalidated the snapshot the previous evidence was taken on. The second correction is CI run 33069684071, which failed on exactly one assertion and for no capability reason: the restored database published nothing to the host there either, but that daemon reported the absent mapping as {} where the local daemon reported it as {"5432/tcp": null}, so the frozen test had pinned one daemon's wording instead of the invariant. The portable oracle is the second-correction replan now frozen at b59540ee938eac8fc18e2acd25fe98a000c231525351f73814ef347436d51d43 — no port other than 5432/tcp may appear at all and 5432/tcp may never carry a binding, which both spellings satisfy — and that replan changed the snapshot, so the writer's budgeted local run is spent again on the current one. Recorded by the reviewer, not asserted here.
A separate read-only session on this immutable snapshot must accept the package. The writer cannot review the package the writer wrote, and any change to the snapshot invalidates the review.

Deleting tests/_harness/live-recovery-probe.mjs and this manifest (and the frozen test if the whole package is withdrawn) returns the tree to base tree 136dfe6c766630efbceffd5842b209c1ff0b24d8. Every Docker resource the run creates carries that run's unique label and is removed by the same run, and the backup directory is deleted before the process exits, so nothing outside this checkout has to be undone.

environmentPins.restoreSuperuserPasswordDelivery: a raw mode-0600 file bind-mounted READ-ONLY at /run/secrets/postgres-password and named to the pinned image through POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE. --env-file was removed: the CLI reads it on the host and copies its contents into Config.Env, where docker inspect returns the cluster password to anyone who can reach the daemon for as long as the container exists — long after the file on disk is gone. Only the path is recorded in the container.
environmentPins.restoreSecretDeletionOrder: the host secret directory is removed only after the restored cluster answers pg_isready inside the contract bound, because the image reads the file during initdb; deleting it earlier is a restore that never starts rather than a secret withdrawn, and the removal still runs on the failure path.
environmentPins.imageSource: the restored database is served by exactly the pinned image the lost database really ran, read off the environment rather than named again here

rollback.mechanism: Delete tests/_harness/live-recovery-probe.mjs and planning/kernel-disaster-recovery-backup-restore-p23a.json, and the frozen test if the whole package is withdrawn. No existing file was modified, so this restores the base tree exactly.
rollback.blastRadius: Confined to one new test-only probe file plus this manifest and the frozen test. No src module, no host module, no image definition, no schema, no migration, no dependency, no lock, no workflow, no roadmap document and no running system is touched. The database this package backs up, destroys and restores exists only inside an ephemeral environment that deletes itself, and the archive is written into a temporary directory removed before the process exits.
rollback.compensatingStepReason: Nothing outside the run survives it. The destroyed container and volume, the restored container and its fresh volume, the application container, the network, the image tag and the temporary host secret directory all carry the run's unique label and are removed by the unchanged P22B1 teardown; the backup file and its directory are deleted in the same run. Nothing was pushed, deployed, promoted or persisted, so there is no external effect to compensate for.

nonGoals: No high availability and no failover: there is one instance of everything here, and nothing in this package survives a lost node.
No migration rollback and no upgrade rollback drill: the restore lands on exactly the migration head the backup was taken at, and no schema version is ever moved backwards.
No point-in-time recovery and no WAL archiving: this is one archive taken at one instant, and there is no way here to recover to any other instant.
No RPO and no RTO is agreed, measured, implied or claimed; this package proves that a restore works, not how much data or how much time an outage may cost.
No scheduled backup and no offsite copy exists: the archive is taken by one test run, into a temporary directory on the same machine, and deleted before that run exits.
No production and no staging environment exists or is contacted; no production host is selected, no registry is contacted or pushed to, and no deployment or promotion is performed or implied.

No host port is published for the application, the lost database or the restored one; no image is defined, edited or rebuilt, and the restored database is served by exactly the pinned image the lost one already ran.
No src module, host module, schema, migration, dependency, lock, CI workflow or roadmap document is modified, and no readiness flag beyond the declared set is introduced.
capabilityDelta: VERIFIED_BACKUP_AND_RESTORE: this system can now lose its database and get it back, without the recovery itself leaking a credential — the restored cluster's superuser password is a read-only mounted mode-0600 file named by path, so docker inspect returns a path and never a password. A custom-format archive of exactly the business database is taken from the live environment with no credential on any command line and no credential inside the archive, and its sha256 is recomputed from the bytes really on disk. The database container and the data volume under it are then destroyed, so the loss is total — and the still-running listener, still holding a live credential to a database that no longer exists, fails closed with a server error that carries no receipt, claims no commit and discloses neither the password nor any connection string. The archive is restored into a fresh volume served by the same pinned image, and what comes back is the whole truth: the real migration head, exactly the rows that existed before the loss with no row missing and none invented, the two non-superuser roles with row-level security still forced and tenant isolation still in place, a runtime role PostgreSQL still refuses DDL to, and a decision log that still verifies independently by recomputation. Then the untouched listener writes again through the same mounted credential on the same alias, and the new decision chains onto the entry hash the genesis had BEFORE the disaster: one chain across the disaster, not a second one started after it. What this does not add is any of the rest of disaster recovery — no schedule, no offsite copy, no recovery objective, no point-in-time recovery, no failover.

productClaim.runnable: The recovery runs today: `node --test tests/kernel-disaster-recovery-backup-restore-p23a.test.mjs` brings up the unchanged P22B1 environment, commits one trusted POST /customers over live HTTP, takes a verified owner-only backup of exactly the mfk database, destroys the database container and its volume, proves the live listener fails closed without leaking its credential, restores the archive into a fresh volume served by the same pinned image, proves the migration head, the rows, the roles, the forced row-level security and the decision chain all came back, and commits a second write that chains onto the pre-disaster genesis — leaving zero labelled resources and no archive on disk.
productClaim.notRunnable: There is still no runnable product, and this is not a disaster-recovery plan. There is no user interface, no persistent database, no hosted environment and no way for a real person to reach this listener; the backup is taken by hand inside one test run and deleted with it, so there is no schedule, no retention, no offsite copy and no monitored recovery drill. Nothing here recovers to a point in time, rolls a migration back or survives a lost node, and no recovery objective has been agreed with anyone. P23 stays open until P23B and P23C exist and P23D closes it, and every readiness flag beyond the six declared true — deployAllowed, productionAllowed, stagingEnvironmentExists, runnableProduct and p23Complete among them — stays false.

userJourney.once: Önceden sistem gerçek bir müşteri kaydını gerçekten yazıyordu, ama o kaydın tutulduğu veritabanı test biter bitmez siliniyordu ve bugüne kadar o veritabanından hiçbir şey dışarı alınıp geri konmamıştı. Yani 'veriyi kaybedersek geri gelir mi' sorusunun bu depoda hiçbir cevabı yoktu: denenmemiş bir yedek yedek değildir, hiç yapılmamış bir geri yükleme ise sadece bir umuttur.
userJourney.simdi: Şimdi önce gerçek bir müşteri kaydı yazılıyor, sonra tam olarak o veritabanının doğrulanabilir bir yedeği alınıyor: dosyanın parmak izi diskteki baytlardan yeniden hesaplanıyor, dosya sadece sahibinin okuyabileceği izinle yazılıyor ve yedeğin içinde hiçbir şifre bulunmuyor. Ardından veritabanı konteyneri ve altındaki veri birimi tamamen siliniyor, yedek taze bir birime geri yükleniyor ve geri gelenin eksiksiz olduğu sunucudan okunarak kanıtlanıyor.
userJourney.fark: Fark iki yerde en net görülüyor. Birincisi kayıp anı: veritabanı yokken gelen istek sessizce 'kaydettim' demiyor, açık bir hatayla kapanıyor ve elinde hâlâ tuttuğu veritabanı şifresini ne cevabında ne de bir bağlantı adresinde dışarı sızdırmıyor. İkincisi geri dönüş anı: geri yüklemeden sonra yazılan yeni kayıt, felaketten ÖNCEKİ denetim halkasının parmak izine bağlanıyor — yani zincir kopmuyor, ikinci bir zincir başlamıyor. Üçüncü bir fark da kurtarmanın kendisinde: geri yüklenen veritabanının yönetici şifresi artık hiçbir yerde ortada durmuyor. Şifre sadece sahibinin okuyabileceği bir dosyaya yazılıyor, kaba salt-okunur bağlanıyor ve sisteme değeri değil YOLU söyleniyor; sunucuyu sorgulayan biri şifreyi değil yalnızca dosyanın yolunu görüyor, dosyanın kendisi de veritabanı ayağa kalkar kalkmaz siliniyor.
userJourney.kullaniciYolculugu: Bir CRM kullanıcısının müşteri formunu doldurup kaydettiğini düşünün. Kayıt oluşuyor. Sonra veritabanı tamamen kayboluyor: kullanıcı yeni bir kayıt denediğinde sistem yalan söylemiyor, açıkça hata veriyor. Yedek geri yükleniyor ve aynı kullanıcı hiçbir şey yapmadan, aynı ayarla, aynı adrese yazmaya devam edebiliyor; eski müşterisi kayıp değil, yerinde duruyor ve yeni kayıt onun üstüne ekleniyor. Ama bu kullanıcı hâlâ yok: ekran yok, kalıcı ortam yok, erişilebilir bir adres yok; yedek de tek bir test koşusu içinde elle alınıp aynı koşuda siliniyor.
userJourney.kalanEngel: Kalan engel açık: burada yedek takvimi yok, başka bir makinede kopya yok, 'en fazla ne kadar veri kaybedilebilir, en fazla ne kadar sürede geri dönülür' diye anlaşılmış bir hedef yok, belirli bir ana geri dönme yok, sürüm geri alma yok ve düğüm kaybına dayanma yok. P23 fazı ancak P23B ile P23C yapılıp P23D yol haritasını kapattığında kapanır; yayına alma ile ilgili hiçbir bayrak kalkmadı.

residualRisks: A one-database archive cannot carry cluster-level roles, so the two non-superuser roles are re-created on the restored cluster before the archive is loaded, with the runtime password read from the credential file the listener still holds. That is the honest procedure for this shape of backup — and the reason the frozen test asserts the restored role flags against pg_roles rather than trusting the probe.

The recovery is proven once, by hand, inside an environment that deletes itself. Nothing here shows that a backup taken tomorrow restores, that a larger database restores inside any bound, or that anyone would notice a failed backup: there is no schedule, no retention, no offsite copy and no monitoring.

The verification reads run as the database superuser, which bypasses row-level security. That is deliberate and is the only way a sweep can prove a row absent rather than merely invisible; the listener still reaches its own data as the NOBYPASSRLS runtime role, and this package changes no privilege of that role.
The environment, its digest pin and its Docker hard requirement are P22B1's and are unchanged here: a docker-unavailable failure is an environment failure and never a P23A capability gap.
